claim: Hair cells of the cochlea are mechanosensors for the perception of sound.
source: Hair cells of the cochlea are mechanosensors for the perception of sound.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in auditory neuroscience, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Mutations in the LRTOMT gene cause deafness.
source: Mutations in the LRTOMT gene, which encodes a protein with homology to the catecholamine methyltransferase COMT that is linked to schizophrenia, cause deafness.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Ahmed et al., 2008; Du et al., 2008) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: LRTOMT encodes a protein with homology to the catecholamine methyltransferase COMT.
source: Mutations in the LRTOMT gene, which encodes a protein with homology to the catecholamine methyltransferase COMT that is linked to schizophrenia, cause deafness.
evidence: This is based on sequence homology analysis, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: COMT is linked to schizophrenia.
source: Mutations in the LRTOMT gene, which encodes a protein with homology to the catecholamine methyltransferase COMT that is linked to schizophrenia, cause deafness.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Männistö and Kaakkola, 1999; Tunbridge, 2010) in the introduction.

claim: Tomt/Comt2 is the murine ortholog of LRTOMT.
source: Here, we show that Tomt/Comt2, the murine ortholog of LRTOMT, has an unexpected function in the regulation of mechanotransduction by hair cells.
evidence: This is based on sequence homology and comparative genomics, representing established knowledge.

claim: The role of mTOMT in hair cells is independent of mTOMT methyltransferase function.
source: The role of mTOMT in hair cells is independent of mTOMT methyltransferase function and mCOMT cannot substitute for mTOMT function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7, showing that mutations affecting methyltransferase activity do not prevent rescue of mechanotransduction.

claim: mCOMT cannot substitute for mTOMT function.
source: The role of mTOMT in hair cells is independent of mTOMT methyltransferase function and mCOMT cannot substitute for mTOMT function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing that mCOMT-GFP cannot rescue mechanotransduction defects in Tomt mutants.

claim: mTOMT binds to putative components of the mechanotransduction channel in hair cells.
source: Instead, mTOMT binds to putative components of the mechanotransduction channel in hair cells and is essential for the transport of some of these components into the mechanically sensitive stereocilia of hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: mTOMT is essential for the transport of some mechanotransduction channel components into stereocilia.
source: Instead, mTOMT binds to putative components of the mechanotransduction channel in hair cells and is essential for the transport of some of these components into the mechanically sensitive stereocilia of hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by injectoporation experiments in Figure 8 showing that TMC1 and TMC2 fail to localize to stereocilia in Tomt mutants.

claim: Defects in the assembly of the mechanotransduction machinery are likely mechanistically linked to deafness caused by mutations in LRTOMT/Tomt.
source: Defects in this process are likely mechanistically linked to deafness caused by mutations in LRTOMT/Tomt.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing mechanotransduction defects in Tomt mutants.

claim: Each hair cell contains at the apical surface a bundle of stereocilia that are organized in rows of decreasing height.
source: Each hair cell contains at the apical surface a bundle of stereocilia that are organized in rows of decreasing height (Alagramam et al., 2011; Schwander et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Tip links connect the stereocilia of hair cells in the direction of their mechanical sensitivity.
source: Tip links connect the stereocilia of hair cells in the direction of their mechanical sensitivity and are thought to transmit force onto transduction channels that are situated near the lower end of tip links (Figure 1A) (Assad et al., 1991; Pickles et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Tip links transmit force onto transduction channels situated near the lower end of tip links.
source: Tip links connect the stereocilia of hair cells in the direction of their mechanical sensitivity and are thought to transmit force onto transduction channels that are situated near the lower end of tip links (Figure 1A) (Assad et al., 1991; Pickles et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a widely accepted model in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Tip links consist of CDH23 homodimers that interact in trans with PCDH15 homodimers.
source: Tip links consist of CDH23 homodimers that interact in trans with PCDH15 homodimers to form the upper and lower part of tip links, respectively (Figure 1A) (Ahmed et al., 2006; Kazmierczak et al., 2007; Siemens et al., 2004; Söllner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The adaptor proteins harmonin and SANS, and the molecular motor myosin 7a (MYO7A), bind to the CDH23 cytoplasmic domain.
source: The adaptor proteins harmonin and SANS, and the molecular motor myosin 7a (MYO7A), bind to the CDH23 cytoplasmic domain (Adato et al., 2005; Bahloul et al., 2010; Boëda et al., 2002; Siemens et al., 2002) and co-localize near the cytoplasmic domain of CDH23 at the upper tip-link density (UTLD) (Figure 1A), an electron-dense area near the insertion site of CDH23 into the stereociliary membrane (Grati and Kachar, 2011; Grillet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: TMHS/LHFPL5, TMIE and TMC1/2 are localized near PCDH15 at the lower tip-link density (LTLD).
source: TMHS/LHFPL5, TMIE and TMC1/2 are localized near PCDH15 at the lower tip-link density (LTLD) (Figure 1A), an electron dense area at the tips of stereocilia (Kurima et al., 2015; Xiong et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TMHS/LHFPL5, TMIE and TMC1/2 are candidate proteins to be components of the mechanotransduction channel in hair cells.
source: TMHS/LHFPL5, TMIE and TMC1/2 are candidate proteins to be components of the mechanotransduction channel in hair cells (Kawashima et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2013; Xiong et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanotransduction machinery of hair cells shows a striking asymmetry with distinct protein complexes present at the upper and lower end of tip links.
source: Thus, the mechanotransduction machinery of hair cells shows a striking asymmetry with distinct protein complexes present at the upper and lower end of tip links.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data cited in the preceding sentences.

claim: Tomt is prominently expressed in cochlear hair cells.
source: We have previously shown by in situ hybridization that Tomt is prominently expressed in cochlear hair cells (Du et al., 2008), suggesting that Tomt directly regulates hair cell function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Tomt directly regulates hair cell function.
source: We have previously shown by in situ hybridization that Tomt is prominently expressed in cochlear hair cells (Du et al., 2008), suggesting that Tomt directly regulates hair cell function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and the phenotype of mutants.

claim: mTOMT is expressed in the cytoplasm of hair cells.
source: Immunolocalization studies have revealed mTOMT expression in the cytoplasm of hair cells and potentially additional expression in support cells that was not revealed by in situ hybridization (Ahmed et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Add mice carry a point mutation (R48L) in the Tomt gene.
source: Add mice carry a point mutation (R48L) in the Tomt gene (referred to as Tomtadd) (Figure 1D,F,I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and prior work (Du et al., 2008).

claim: Recombinant mTOMT has catechola-O-methyltransferase activity in vitro.
source: Our previous studies have shown that recombinant mTOMT has catechola-O-methyltransferase activity in vitro, although the methyltransferase activity is significantly less compared to mCOMT.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Du et al., 2008).

claim: The methyltransferase activity of mTOMT is significantly less compared to mCOMT.
source: Our previous studies have shown that recombinant mTOMT has catechola-O-methyltransferase activity in vitro, although the methyltransferase activity is significantly less compared to mCOMT.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Du et al., 2008).

claim: The add mutation reduces methyltransferase activity.
source: The add mutation reduces methyltransferase activity but could also affect protein stability (Du et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The add mutation could affect protein stability.
source: The add mutation reduces methyltransferase activity but could also affect protein stability (Du et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculation based on the nature of the mutation.

claim: The TomtD12 mutation carries a 12 base pair in-frame deletion near the N-terminus.
source: One of the CRISPR-engineered alleles, referred to as TomtD12, carries a 12 base pair (bp) in-frame deletion near the N-terminus (Figure 1E–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Tomtdel allele carries a deletion of 77 bp leading to a frame-shift and premature stop codon near the N-terminus of mTOMT.
source: The second allele, Tomtdel, carries a deletion of 77 bp leading to a frame-shift and premature stop codon near the N-terminus of mTOMT (Figure 1E–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The TomtD12 mutation is predicted to produce a protein with an internal deletion of 4 amino acids.
source: While the TomtD12 mutation is predicted to produce a protein with an internal deletion of 4 amino acids, the Tomtdel mutation is predicted to generate a functional null allele.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DNA sequence changes shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Tomtdel mutation is predicted to generate a functional null allele.
source: While the TomtD12 mutation is predicted to produce a protein with an internal deletion of 4 amino acids, the Tomtdel mutation is predicted to generate a functional null allele.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DNA sequence changes shown in Figure 1.

claim: ABR thresholds to broadband click stimuli of control wild-type animals were at 26 ± 3 dB.
source: The ABR thresholds to broadband click stimuli of control wild-type animals were at 26 ± 3 dB (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ABR responses to click stimuli were absent in all mutant mouse lines even at 90 dB.
source: In contrast, ABR responses to click stimuli were absent in all mutant mouse lines even at 90 dB, demonstrating that the mice were profoundly deaf (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Homozygous Tomtadd/add, TomtD12/D12 and Tomtdel/del mice were profoundly deaf.
source: In contrast, ABR responses to click stimuli were absent in all mutant mouse lines even at 90 dB, demonstrating that the mice were profoundly deaf (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ABR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Homozygous Tomtadd/add, TomtD12/D12 and Tomtdel/del mice were deaf across the entire analyzed frequency spectrum.
source: Recordings of ABRs in response to pure tones revealed that homozygous Tomtadd/add, TomtD12/D12 and Tomtdel/del mice were deaf across the entire analyzed frequency spectrum (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hearing function was not significantly affected in 4-week-old heterozygous Tomtadd/+, TomtD12/+ and Tomtdel/+ mice.
source: Hearing function was not significantly affected in 4-week-old heterozygous Tomtadd/+, TomtD12/+ and Tomtdel/+ mice (data not shown), consistent with a recessive mode of inheritance of the auditory phenotype.
evidence: This is experimental data, though not shown in a figure.

claim: The auditory phenotype in Tomt mutants shows a recessive mode of inheritance.
source: Hearing function was not significantly affected in 4-week-old heterozygous Tomtadd/+, TomtD12/+ and Tomtdel/+ mice (data not shown), consistent with a recessive mode of inheritance of the auditory phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that heterozygotes have normal hearing.

claim: DPOAEs were absent in Tomtadd/add and TomtD12/D12 at 4 weeks of age at all frequencies tested.
source: DPOAEs were absent in Tomtadd/add and TomtD12/D12 at 4 weeks of age at all frequencies tested (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: OHC function was affected in Tomt mutant mice.
source: As these emissions depend on the mechanical activity of OHCs, we conclude that OHC function was affected in Tomt mutant mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DPOAE data and established knowledge about DPOAEs.

claim: HA-mTOMT, mTOMT-HA and mTOMT-GFP were consistently prominently expressed throughout the cytoplasm of hair cells, but not in their stereocilia.
source: Consistent with previous immunolocalization studies of endogenous proteins (Ahmed et al., 2008) we observed consistently prominent expression of HA-mTOMT, mTOMT-HA and mTOMT-GFP throughout the cytoplasm of hair cells, but not in their stereocilia (Figure 3C, and data not shown).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: mTOMT-GFP was not significantly colocalized with GM130, a marker of Golgi, in heterologous cells or hair cells.
source: mTOMT-GFP was not significantly colocalized with GM130, a marker of Golgi, in heterologous cells or hair cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,D,E).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In heterologous cells, HA-mTOMT and mTOMT-GFP partially co-localized with KDEL, a marker of the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: In heterologous cells, HA-mTOMT and mTOMT-GFP partially co-localized with KDEL, a marker of the endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and EEA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In heterologous cells, HA-mTOMT and mTOMT-GFP partially co-localized with EEA1.
source: In heterologous cells, HA-mTOMT and mTOMT-GFP partially co-localized with KDEL, a marker of the endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and EEA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: LRTOMT2-GFP was localized to the cell body of hair cells and was not present in the stereocilia.
source: LRTOMT2-GFP was also localized to the cell body of hair cells, was not present in the stereocilia (Figure 3D) and had a similar distribution in heterologous cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) suggesting that the subcellular localization of mTOMT and LRTOMT2 is similar and possibly conserved.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The subcellular localization of mTOMT and LRTOMT2 is similar and possibly conserved.
source: LRTOMT2-GFP was also localized to the cell body of hair cells, was not present in the stereocilia (Figure 3D) and had a similar distribution in heterologous cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) suggesting that the subcellular localization of mTOMT and LRTOMT2 is similar and possibly conserved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data.

claim: The sensory epithelia in Tomtadd/add, TomtD12/D12 and Tomtdel/del mutant mice at P5 were patterned into three rows of OHCs and one row of IHCs with no obvious structural abnormalities.
source: Whole mount staining of the dissected sensory epithelium of Tomtadd/add, TomtD12/D12 and Tomtdel/del mice at P5 revealed that the sensory epithelia in mutant mice were patterned into three rows of OHCs and one row of IHCs with no obvious structural abnormalities (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: At P5, the bundles of outer hair cells (OHCs) in homozygous mutants appeared similar in size to those of wild-type mice and formed a normal staircase pattern.
source: At P5, the bundles of outer hair cells (OHCs) in homozygous mutants appeared similar in size to those of wild-type mice and formed a normal staircase pattern (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The hair bundles of OHCs in Tomtadd/add mice had a slightly more rounded morphology, especially in basal regions of the cochlea.
source: With SEM, the hair bundles of OHCs had a slightly more rounded morphology, especially in basal regions of the cochlea (Figure 4E,F,H).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F,H.

claim: The morphology of inner hair cells (IHCs) was not significantly altered in Tomt mutants.
source: The morphology of inner hair cells (IHCs) was not significantly altered (Figure 4A–C,I,J; and data not shown).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: mTOMT is not essential for the initial patterning of the cochlear sensory epithelium and for the development of hair cells and their hair bundles.
source: We thus conclude that mTOMT is not essential for the initial patterning of the cochlear sensory epithelium and for the development of hair cells and their hair bundles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphological data in Figure 4.

claim: Hair cells were maintained in explants from homozygous Tomtdel/del and Tomtadd/add mice even in the presence of Gentamicin.
source: Strikingly, while hair-cell death was nearly complete in explants from control mice cultured in the presence but not absence of Gentamicin (Figure 5A,B), hair cells were maintained in explants from homozygous Tomtdel/del and Tomtadd/add mice even in the presence of Gentamicin (Figure 5C,D), suggesting that mechanotransduction-channel function was defective in the mutants.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Mechanotransduction-channel function was defective in Tomt mutants.
source: Strikingly, while hair-cell death was nearly complete in explants from control mice cultured in the presence but not absence of Gentamicin (Figure 5A,B), hair cells were maintained in explants from homozygous Tomtdel/del and Tomtadd/add mice even in the presence of Gentamicin (Figure 5C,D), suggesting that mechanotransduction-channel function was defective in the mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Gentamicin resistance data.

claim: The amplitude of saturated mechanotransduction currents in control OHCs in the mid-apical part of the cochlea at maximal deflection with a stiff glass probe was at 509 ± 50 pA at P4 and 595 ± 56 pA at P7.
source: The amplitude of saturated mechanotransduction currents in control OHCs in the mid-apical part of the cochlea at maximal deflection with a stiff glass probe was at 509 ± 50 pA (mean ± SEM) at P4 and 595 ± 56 pA at P7 (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: Transducer currents were very small (45 ± 6 pA) in P4 hair cells from Tomtadd/add mice.
source: In contrast, transducer currents were very small (45 ± 6 pA) in P4 hair cells and completely absent in P7 hair cells from Tomtadd/add mice, even at maximal deflection of their bundles (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Transducer currents were completely absent in P7 hair cells from Tomtadd/add mice.
source: In contrast, transducer currents were very small (45 ± 6 pA) in P4 hair cells and completely absent in P7 hair cells from Tomtadd/add mice, even at maximal deflection of their bundles (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Membrane potential, outward-evoked currents and nonlinear capacitance were normal in OHCs from Tomtadd/add mice.
source: Membrane potential, outward-evoked currents and nonlinear capacitance were normal in OHCs from Tomtadd/add mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the mechanotransduction defects were not a secondary consequence of another process affecting the overall health of the hair cells.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mechanotransduction defects in Tomt mutants were not a secondary consequence of another process affecting the overall health of the hair cells.
source: Membrane potential, outward-evoked currents and nonlinear capacitance were normal in OHCs from Tomtadd/add mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the mechanotransduction defects were not a secondary consequence of another process affecting the overall health of the hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: There was no difference in the expression or localization of CDH23, PCDH15, PMCA, MYO7A, Espin and Whirlin between wild-type and Tomt mutant mice at P5-P8.
source: We did not observe any difference in the expression or localization of these proteins between wild-type and mutant mice at P5-P8.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in the number of tip links between wild-type and Tomtadd/add mice.
source: There was no statistically significant difference in the number of tip links between wild-type and Tomtadd/add mice (Figure 6M,N).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 6M,N.

claim: The mechanotransduction defects in Tomt-deficient mice are not primarily caused by defects in tip-link assembly.
source: We conclude that the mechanotransduction defects in Tomt-deficient mice are not primarily caused by defects in tip-link assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tip-link quantification data.

claim: COMT regulates catecholamine levels in the brain.
source: COMT regulates catecholamine levels in the brain and recombinant mTOMT has previously been shown to have catecholamine-O-methyltransferase activity in vitro, albeit significantly less than COMT (Du et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: None of the tested catecholamines or inhibitors prevented Gentamicin-induced hair cell death.
source: None of the tested catecholamines or inhibitors prevented Gentamicin-induced hair cell death (Figure 7B–K), suggesting that mechanotransduction was not directly affected by these catecholamines or changes in global methyltransferase activity.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 7B-K.

claim: Mechanotransduction was not directly affected by catecholamines or changes in global methyltransferase activity.
source: None of the tested catecholamines or inhibitors prevented Gentamicin-induced hair cell death (Figure 7B–K), suggesting that mechanotransduction was not directly affected by these catecholamines or changes in global methyltransferase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Gentamicin experiments.

claim: Catecholamines did not have noticeable effects on mechanotransduction as evaluated by patch-clamp electrophysiology.
source: Analysis of the effects of catecholamines on mechanotransduction was also evaluated by patch-clamp electrophysiology with no noticeable effects on mechanotransduction (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Norepinephrine, homovanillic acid (HVA) and serotonin were detected in the inner ear with no significant difference between wild-type and Tomtadd/add animals.
source: We detected norepinephrine, homovanillic acid (HVA) and norepinephrine with no significant difference between wild-type and mutant animals (Figure 7M).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 7M.

claim: Mechanotransduction defects were not rescued by expression of mTOMT-MT-GFP or mCOMT-GFP.
source: Mechanotransduction defects were not rescued by expression of mTOMT-MT-GFP (32 ± 3 pA) or mCOMT-GFP (40 ± 0.5 pA).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 7O-Q.

claim: mTOMT-GFP and mTOMT-Y108A-GFP rescued transduction to a similar extent.
source: In contrast, mTOMT-GFP (231 ± 19 pA) and mTOMT-Y108A-GFP (278 ± 41 pA) rescued transduction to a similar extent.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 7O-Q.

claim: Methyltransferase activity is not essential for TOMT function in hair cells.
source: Nevertheless, the fact that both mTOMT-GFP and mTOMT-Y108A-GFP rescued transduction to a similar extent, while the methyltransferase mCOMT-GFP or the putative TOMT methyltransferase domain (mTOMT-MT-GFP) could not, suggests that methyltransferase activity is not essential for TOMT function in hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments in Figure 7.

claim: TOMT-FLAG or TOMT-HA could be co-immunoprecipitated with Myc-TMC1, Myc-TMC2, TMIE-HA, HA-TMHS/LHFPL5 and PCDH15, but not with CDH23.
source: Significantly, epitope-tagged versions of TOMT (TOMT-FLAG or TOMT-HA) could be co-immunoprecipitated with Myc-TMC1, Myc-TMC2, TMIE-HA, HA-TMHS/LHFPL5 and PCDH15, but not with CDH23 (Figure 8A–E, data not shown).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 8A-E.

claim: TOMT was not essential for PCDH15 transport.
source: Our analysis of tip-link cadherins (Figure 6) already suggested that TOMT was not essential for PCDH15 transport.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunolocalization data in Figure 6.

claim: TOMT did not have obvious effects on the distribution of TMHS/LHFPL5.
source: To evaluate distribution of TMHS/LHFPL5, we carried out immunolocalization studies in hair cells from wild-types and mutants but did not observe any obvious effect of TOMT on the distribution of TMHS/LHFPL5 (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: TMIE-HA was effectively targeted to the hair bundles of wild-type and Tomt-deficient animals.
source: TMIE-HA was effectively targeted to the hair bundles of wild-type and Tomt-deficient animals (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Both Myc-TMC1 and Myc-TMC2 were absent from the stereocilia of Tomt-deficient hair cells.
source: Strikingly, both Myc-TMC1 and Myc-TMC2 were absent from the stereocilia of Tomt-deficient hair cells (Figure 8H,I,K).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 8H,I,K.

claim: When mTOMT-GFP was coexpressed with Myc-Tmc2 in Tomt-deficient hair cells, Myc-Tmc2 stereociliary localization was rescued.
source: When mTOMT-GFP was coexpressed with Myc-Tmc2 in Tomt-deficient hair cells, Myc-Tmc2 stereociliary localization was rescued (Figure 8J,K).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 8J,K.

claim: In hair cells, TOMT is essential to regulate the transport of TMC1 and TMC2 into stereocilia.
source: These findings suggest that in hair cells, TOMT is essential to regulate the transport of TMC1 and TMC2 into stereocilia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the injectoporation experiments in Figure 8.

claim: TMC1 and TMC2 cannot be effectively expressed at the cell surface in heterologous cells such as HEK293 cells or COS-7 cells.
source: Notably, previous studies have shown that in heterologous cells such as HEK293 cells or COS-7 cells, TMC1 and TMC2 cannot be effectively expressed at the cell surface; instead, the proteins appear to be retained intracellularly, likely within the endoplasmic reticulum (Beurg et al., 2015; Labay et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Co-expression of TOMT-GFP or HA-TOMT did not alter the distribution of TMC1 and TMC2 in COS-7 cells.
source: Co-expression of TOMT-GFP or HA-TOMT did not alter the distribution of TMC1 and TMC2 in COS-7 cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, and data not shown), suggesting that TOMT alone is not sufficient to regulate the transport of TMC1 and TMC2 to the cell membrane.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: TOMT alone is not sufficient to regulate the transport of TMC1 and TMC2 to the cell membrane.
source: Co-expression of TOMT-GFP or HA-TOMT did not alter the distribution of TMC1 and TMC2 in COS-7 cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, and data not shown), suggesting that TOMT alone is not sufficient to regulate the transport of TMC1 and TMC2 to the cell membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the heterologous cell expression data.

claim: Reverse polarity currents depend on PIEZO2 ion channels that are localized near the base of stereocilia.
source: These reverse polarity currents depend on the PIEZO2 ion channel that is concentrated near the base of stereocilia (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Both normal and reverse polarity currents are affected by mTOMT.
source: We were therefore surprised that both normal and reverse polarity currents are affected by mTOMT.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Normal polarity currents and reverse polarity currents were not observed in OHCs from Tomtadd/add mutants without BAPTA treatment.
source: We recorded regular normal-polarity currents in hair cells from P4 control Tomtadd/+ mice (Figure 9A,B). Small normal-polarity currents were also observed in P4 Tomtadd/add mutants (Figure 9A,B), similar to results obtained when hair cells were stimulated at P4 with a stiff glass probe (Figures 5 and 7). However, unlike OHCs from any other mutant mouse strain with defects in mechanotransduction, we did not observe reverse polarity currents in OHCs from Tomtadd/add mutants (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Reverse polarity currents of similar amplitude could be evoked in hair cells from controls and Tomtadd/add mutants after treatment with BAPTA.
source: Surprisingly, reverse polarity currents of similar amplitude could be evoked in hair cells from controls and Tomtadd/add mutants after treatment with BAPTA (Figure 9A,C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 9A,C.

claim: Loss of TMC stereociliary localization alone is not sufficient to induce reverse polarity currents.
source: This result is striking and suggests that loss of TMC stereociliary localization alone is not sufficient to induce reverse polarity currents and that mTOMT is essential for the process of inducing reverse polarity currents in TMC mutant animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reverse polarity current data in Figure 9.

claim: mTOMT is essential for the process of inducing reverse polarity currents in TMC mutant animals.
source: This result is striking and suggests that loss of TMC stereociliary localization alone is not sufficient to induce reverse polarity currents and that mTOMT is essential for the process of inducing reverse polarity currents in TMC mutant animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reverse polarity current data in Figure 9.

claim: mTOMT has a critical role in the generation of reverse polarity currents downstream of TMC.
source: Thus, mTOMT has a critical role in the generation of reverse polarity currents downstream of TMC (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the reverse polarity current data.

claim: A significant number of the genes linked to deafness encode proteins that directly affect mechanotransduction.
source: A significant number of the genes linked to deafness encode proteins that directly affect mechanotransduction (Kazmierczak and Müller, 2012; Zhao and Müller, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A subset of hearing disorders can be classified as mechanotransduction diseases.
source: These findings suggest that a subset of hearing disorders can be classified as mechanotransduction diseases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that many deafness genes affect mechanotransduction.

claim: mTOMT acts independently of its enzymatic function in regulating the localization of TMC1/2.
